newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand says to study if IMF credit line needed.
newsitem.headline: Thailand says to study if IMF credit line needed.

text.p: Thailand said on Monday that it would, among a host of other economic rescue measures, study if a standby IMF credit line was necessary for the country to help it overcome a financial crisis and liquidity problems.

Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya told a news conference that the issue would be raised in a rehabilitation package now under consideration by the government. The much-awaited package, which was being studied by economic ministers would first be sent to the cabinet for approval by August 5, the minister said.
"The question of whether we need a standby IMF credit line will be included in the package (drawn up by the finance minister)," he said, without saying how much credit would be needed.

Thailand, which is facing its worst economic crisis in over a decade, has been urged by economists, analysts and prominent local businessmen to seek IMF financial assistance to overcome its woes. The government had initially been reluctant to do so.
But Thanong revealed that Thailand had indeed been seeking IMF counsel and advice for the past month because it lacked the expertise or experience to resolve its economic problems.

He added that his economic rehabilitation package when approved would improve Thailand's credit rating among investors, build confidence in the country and its ability to service its debt as well as create an atmosphere for the rolling over of loans to Thai business.
"The package will touch on this issue because a standby credit from the IMF could help stabilise the baht and tackle the liquidity problem. This is all part of the framework in the package," he said.
"The package will also try to ensure that we will have sufficient foreign reserves that can help stabilise our currency," he added.

Thanong said recent financial measures such as allowing the managed float of the baht on July 2 and policies to allow foreign investors to take more than a 25 percent stake in Thai financial institutions had been done in consultation with IMF.
He added that a five-member IMF team had now arrived in Thailand from Washington and he would hold further consultations with them for advice on how to put the tottering economy on a right track.

"The IMF has a job to help and advice on how to resolve these (Thai) problems systematically...we need their expertise and we want the correct approach extended by the international community," he said.
"We must frankly admit we need expertise and experience in salvaging our problems," he added.
Thanong said Thailand's economic slowdown was due to a liquidity problem and currency instability which led to problems in lending in the local financial system.

"IMF officials still expressed confidence in the Thai economic fundamentals and they believe that Thailand is still in a sound position, especially in its high-savings rate which still can help sustain positive economic growth," he added.
They believed that Thailand was still better than many other countries.
When asked to identify an appropriate level for the baht, he said the issue needed to be discussed with the IMF taking into account the fast-changing fundamentals of the Thai economy.
